1268.title: Two kinds of attention
1268.hook: focused attention on one object, and open monitoring of whatever arises (Lutz et al.)
1268.howItsDone: Some meditation teachers begin students with focused attention on the breath to steady the mind, then introduce open awareness of whatever arises; researchers study the two styles separately because they seem to train different skills.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wandering isn't all bad: the drifting mind can plan and find answers, especially when it knows it's drifting. Your line was wander on purpose.

A camera has two ways of seeing. Zoom in, and one face fills the frame, sharp to every eyelash, while the background melts away. Pull back to the wide shot, and the whole street is there at once: the bus, the pigeons, the woman with the umbrella, nothing in particular in focus and everything in view. Neither is the right way. They're different tools. A group of researchers looking at meditation described it in terms of the same two shots.
screen: `ZOOM IN: ONE FACE.` → `PULL BACK: THE WHOLE STREET.` → `TWO SHOTS, TWO TOOLS.`

segments.voice: Antoine Lutz, Heleen Slagter, John Dunne and Richard Davidson wrote a paper on attention in meditation and described two broad styles. The first is focused attention. You choose one object, the breath at the nostrils, a sound, a word, and rest there. When the mind wanders, you notice, let go of the distraction, and come back: William James's turn back, done on purpose. The skills it trains are narrow and strong: holding on, catching the drift, returning. The second is open monitoring. There's no single object. You rest in awareness and notice whatever arises, a sound, an itch, a worry, a memory, without grabbing it or pushing it away. Then the next thing. The skill here is wide: seeing the whole street without reacting. The authors drew on Buddhist practice for these descriptions. They say these are broad families, not the only kinds of meditation, and that practices can mix them. They also describe focused attention as a common way in: steadying the mind first can make open monitoring easier. Bringing it back is focused attention; catching the idling mind, or wandering on purpose and knowing it, comes closer to open monitoring. One narrows the beam, one widens it, and a meditator, like a good photographer, learns when to zoom and when to pull back.

segments.voice: Spend about a minute in focus: rest on the breath at the nostrils, and when the mind drifts, notice and come back. Then open: let go of the breath as an anchor and let whatever shows up, a sound, a sensation, a thought, come and go like people crossing a wide street, watching without following any of them.
Two kinds of attention. Focused attention rests on one object and returns to it; open monitoring watches whatever arises without grabbing. Today's word.
Your line: focus, then open. Two shots, two tools, and both are attention. Rest well.

1269.title: Can attention grow?
1269.hook: after a three-month retreat, meditators improved at fine visual attention tasks (MacLean et al.)
1269.howItsDone: Researchers test whether meditation trains attention by measuring people on demanding computer tasks before and after practice, and comparing them with a group that hasn't practiced yet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two kinds of attention: focused attention on one object, and open monitoring of whatever arises. Your line was focus, then open.

A piano tuner leans in, strikes a key, and hears that it's a hair flat. To an untrained ear it sounds fine. A birder hears three notes in a hedge and names the bird without seeing it. That kind of hearing is learned. So here's the question William James left open when he said this ideal was easier to define than to train: can attention itself be trained like an ear, not just used but made sharper? Today, one study that tried to find out.

segments.voice: A team led by the psychologist Katherine MacLean studied people on an intensive three-month meditation retreat, with long hours of practice each day, much of it focused attention on the breath. A comparison group waited to do the same retreat later. Before, during and after, both groups did a demanding visual task: lines flashed up one after another, and the job was to catch the rare line slightly shorter than the rest. It's dull, and that's the point. It tests whether attention can stay sharp and steady over time. The result: the retreat group got better at telling the short lines from the long ones, and better at staying sharp as the task wore on. When the comparison group later did its own retreat, it showed gains too. So the honest answer, at least from this study, is yes. Attention can grow. Now the honest limits. This was an intensive retreat, not a few minutes before work. The task was a lab task, not a whole life. And one study needs others to agree with it. But it points somewhere: at least the kind of attention this task measured isn't simply fixed. It responded to practice, the way a tuner's ear does, a lab looking from the outside at something meditators talk about from the inside.

1270.title: The attentional blink
1270.hook: after three months of practice, meditators missed fewer quick-following signals (Slagter et al.)
1270.howItsDone: Researchers measure the attentional blink by flashing a rapid stream of letters with two hidden targets and checking how often the second is missed; in Vipassana-style practice, meditators train noticing whatever arises and letting it pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, can attention grow: after an intensive retreat, meditators got sharper and steadier at a demanding task. Your line was it can grow.

Letters flash in the middle of a screen, one after another, very fast. Hidden among them are two numbers, and the task is to report both. The first number appears, and you catch it. The second comes a split second later, and often it simply isn't there for you. The eyes saw it. The mind didn't. It's as if attention blinked while still busy with the first. Psychologists gave it exactly that name: the attentional blink.
screen: `LETTERS FLASHING FAST.` → `TWO NUMBERS HIDDEN.` → `THE SECOND ONE VANISHES.`

segments.voice: The blink shows that attention is limited not only in space, one thing at a time, but also in time. Catching something seems to take a moment of processing, and while the mind holds on to the first catch, the next can slip by. Some researchers had treated it as a fixed limit of how minds work. Then Heleen Slagter and her colleagues, including Richard Davidson, tested people before and after a three-month meditation retreat in the Vipassana style, a practice of watching whatever arises. A comparison group did the same tests without the retreat. After the retreat, the meditators blinked less: they caught the second number more often. The brain recordings suggested why. When the first number appeared, the meditators' brains seemed to spend fewer resources on it, leaving more room for what came next. Notice how they improved: not by grabbing harder, but by grabbing less. They noticed the first thing and let it go a little sooner. That fits open monitoring: see what arises, don't cling, stay ready for the next. And it reaches past a lab screen. A sharp word at breakfast, held on to all morning, can blink out the small signals that follow: a child's quiet face, a friend's text that needed an answer. Honest limits, as always: one study, a lab task, an intensive retreat. But the shape is worth carrying. Less clinging to the first thing. Fewer blinks for the next.
screen: `LIMITED IN TIME, TOO.` · `A RETREAT, AND FEWER BLINKS.` · `NOT GRABBING HARDER: GRABBING LESS.` · `ROOM FOR WHAT COMES NEXT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath sit in the background and open your attention to the small things that come and go: a click in the wall, a shift in the light, a twinge in the shoulder. Note each one and let it go quickly, so you're ready for the next, and see how much you catch when you aren't still holding the last.
The attentional blink. The moment after catching one thing when the mind misses the next. In one retreat study, meditators blinked less. Today's word.
Your line: fewer blinks. Grabbing less, not harder, leaves room for what comes next. See you soon.

1271.title: The phone on the table
1271.hook: a study found a phone's mere presence reduced working memory, though later studies are mixed (Ward et al.)
1271.howItsDone: Researchers test the mere-presence effect by placing participants' phones on the desk, in a pocket or bag, or in another room, then comparing scores on working memory tasks; results across later studies have been mixed.

Dinner with a friend. Two plates, two glasses, and a phone lying face down by the bread, silent. Nobody touches it the whole meal. It doesn't buzz once. So it isn't doing anything, right? A team of researchers wondered whether that was true. Not a phone that rings or lights up. A phone that does nothing at all, except be there.

segments.voice: Adrian Ward and his colleagues gave people demanding tasks that use working memory, the mind's small scratchpad for holding things while you think. Some people left their phones face down on the desk, silenced. Some put them in a pocket or a bag. Some left them in another room. Those whose phones were in another room did best; those with the phone on the desk did worst. And the strange part: people said the phone wasn't on their mind. The researchers' idea was that some attention goes into not checking it, a quiet, steady effort to ignore something that matters to us, and that effort uses some of the same limited capacity these past days have explored. They called their paper Brain Drain. Now the honest part, and it matters. Later studies have been mixed. Some found a similar effect; others tried and didn't. So this is not settled science, and anyone who says a phone on the table definitely makes you less smart is saying more than the evidence does. But look at what the idea asks us to notice. Attention is limited. Wandering costs. Holding on to the first thing makes us miss the next. A silent phone may be one more pull on that limited supply. And the fix the study points to costs nothing. Not willpower. Not a new app. Just distance. Another room.

1272.title: Switching costs
1272.hook: switching between tasks costs time and accuracy, even when it seems fast
1272.howItsDone: People who take task-switching research to heart often batch their email and messages into set times of day, and some contemplative teachers frame doing one thing at a time as a practice in its own right.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the phone on the table: even a silent phone in view may quietly draw on attention. Your line was another room.

Three tabs open. An email half written. A text that just buzzed. A spreadsheet waiting underneath it all. A glance here, a reply there, back to the email, over to the sheet. To the person doing it, this can seem nimble, even fast. Psychologists who study attention have a dry name for what all that hopping charges you: switching costs. People asked to swap back and forth between two simple jobs get slower and make more mistakes than people who stay with one. And the charge is quiet. The switch seems instant. The bill arrives later, in small coins.
screen: `THREE TABS AND A BUZZING TEXT.` → `IT SEEMS FAST.` → `THE BILL ARRIVES IN SMALL COINS.`

segments.voice: In a common kind of task-switching study, people see a number or a letter and make a quick judgment about it. Sometimes the rule stays the same from one trial to the next; sometimes it changes. When it changes, answers come more slowly and with more errors. Researchers call that gap the switch cost. Why? One explanation is that the mind has to put down one set of rules and pick up another, a kind of reloading. A warning that a switch is coming makes the cost smaller, though in some studies a piece of it stays even when people know exactly what's next. Now an old letter. The Roman philosopher Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius about reading too many books and traveling too much, puts it in three words: "Everywhere means nowhere." He wasn't measuring reaction times. He was describing a mind that never settles long enough to arrive. And an honest limit. Lab tasks are tiny, and a real workday is not a lab. How much these small costs add up across an ordinary afternoon is still argued over, and researchers disagree about the size. The modest takeaway: each switch has some price, and some switches are worth paying for. The ones that aren't are often small and automatic, like the glance at a message that could have waited an hour. Fewer switches, chosen on purpose.

1273.title: Attention residue
1273.hook: part of the mind stays on the last task after the switch (Leroy)

segments.voice: Yesterday, switching costs: each change of task charges a little time and accuracy. Your line was one at a time.

The report in front of you gets read, and read again, and nothing goes in. Part of the mind didn't get the memo that it moved. segments.voice: First, the finding. Leroy studied what happens when people leave one task and start another. Thoughts about the first task kept running in the background, and people with more of those leftover thoughts did worse on the next task. She called it attention residue: some of your attention stays stuck to the thing you just left. Second, what makes it stickier. In her studies, residue was stronger when the first task was left unfinished. A half-done job keeps tapping on the shoulder. When people finished it, especially under a little time pressure that pushed them to close it out, the residue was lower. Third, a way to loosen it. In later work, Leroy and a colleague tested something simple: before switching, people wrote a quick plan for where they would pick the task back up. That small note seemed to help the mind let go, as if it trusted the plan to remember so it didn't have to. Fourth, an old echo. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius, in his private notebook, kept urging himself to give full attention to the thing in hand and to set aside every other thought while doing it. He had no lab and no word for residue, but he knew the problem: the mind trailing behind the body, still in the last room. The research doesn't say you can switch with no leftover. It suggests the leftover can shrink, by finishing what you can and writing down what you can't.

1274.title: The use of boredom
1274.hook: some studies suggest boredom can spark creative thinking
1274.howItsDone: Some people who take this research seriously build unplugged gaps into their day, a walk or a wait without a phone, and some contemplative traditions include long stretches of simply sitting with nothing to do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, attention residue: part of the mind stays stuck on the last task, especially an unfinished one. Your line was clear the residue.

A line at the pharmacy. Nobody is moving. The hand goes to the pocket before the mind has decided anything, and the screen lights up. Empty waiting is getting hard to find, because there's almost always something to fill it. So here's an odd question for the end of a week about attention: what if the empty minute is doing a job? What if being bored, a little, now and then, is useful? A small pile of research says it might be.
screen: `A LINE THAT ISN'T MOVING.` → `THE HAND GOES TO THE POCKET.` → `WHAT IF THE EMPTY MINUTE HAS A JOB?`

segments.voice: First, the study people cite. Two researchers, Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman, gave some volunteers a deliberately dull task: copying numbers out of a phone book. Afterward, everyone listed as many uses as they could for a pair of plastic cups. The people who had been bored came up with more ideas. The researchers' suggestion: a bored mind starts to wander, and wandering can turn up new connections. Second, the honest caveat. Later studies have found weaker or mixed results. So the fair summary is that some studies suggest boredom can spark creative thinking. Not a law; a possibility worth testing on yourself. Third, an older voice, one this path met back on day ten. The French thinker Blaise Pascal, in notes later gathered as the Pensées, wrote: "I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber." He wasn't talking about creativity, but about how hard people work to avoid sitting alone with themselves. Fourth, the week: two kinds of attention, whether it can grow, the blink, the phone on the table, the cost of switching, the residue a switch leaves behind. Boredom is the other side of all of it. It's what attention feels like with nothing to grab, and it may be the room where the mind finally gets to roam.
screen: `COPYING A PHONE BOOK.` · `SOME STUDIES, NOT A LAW.` · then, large: `QUIETLY IN THEIR OWN CHAMBER.` · then: `ATTENTION WITH NOTHING TO GRAB.`

segments.voice: Don't follow the breath or do anything at all; just sit with nothing in particular to look at and nothing to accomplish. If the mind gets restless, let it; if it wanders, see where it goes; if it itches for a screen, notice the itch and stay put. Pascal's chamber, for two minutes.
The use of boredom. The idea, from some studies, that an empty, unfilled stretch of time can give the mind room to wander and make new connections. Today's word.
Your line: bored first. The empty minute may have a job. That's all for today.
